title: To disclose or not to disclose: Peer influence and psychological factors in students' use of generative artificial intelligence
source_used: OpenAlex/PubMed abstract; Wiley hybrid OA blocked by a bot check; NTU repository handle gave no reachable file
ft_reason: HE; evidence on whether students disclose GenAI use under disclosure mandates, which bears directly on declaration-based designs (b under Amendment 3); peer-reviewed.
study_design: Mixed methods (hierarchical regression plus thematic analysis)
sample: 409 GenAI-using undergraduates at a Singaporean university

key_findings.finding: Despite disclosure mandates, students often conceal GenAI use; disclosure was best predicted by perceived peer disclosure and comfort with instructors, with moral disengagement weaker.
Non-disclosure reflected adaptation to peer norms and low trust in instructors' interpretation rather than moral negligence.

dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Disclosure depends on trust and normative clarity rather than compliance.

author_recommendations: Build trusting, communicatively transparent settings to support disclosure (not tested)
limitations: Abstract only; self-reported disclosure likelihood at a single university.
redesign_note: Shows the limits of declaration requirements: disclosure is relational and often withheld.

title: Generative AI and the Quality of Student Research Projects
source_used: oa_url (Artificial Societies print-PDF; bilingual Russian/English text)
ft_reason: HE student research projects; proposes assessment criteria and mandatory process reporting; English version included; peer-reviewed journal.
sample: Authors' observations of course-paper and thesis defences in the 2025 summer session (n not reported for confidentiality) plus HEPI survey data

key_findings.finding: Observed student GenAI use ranged from literature-review and editing support to inserting content without source checks, creating stylistic coherence that can be mistaken for epistemic soundness.

Proposes quality criteria (originality, procedural transparency, reproducibility of reasoning, AI-contribution declaration) and mandatory reporting: an AI-use declaration, a portfolio of drafts and prompts, and an explanatory note.

dimensions.capability_verification: Assessment should check that reasoning can be reproduced.
dimensions.process_visibility: Portfolios of intermediate drafts and prompt lists are required.

author_recommendations: Mandatory AI declaration, drafts-and-prompts portfolio and explanatory note (not tested)
limitations: Empirical basis is the authors' expert experience, with unreported numbers.
redesign_note: Proposes revised assessment criteria and process-reporting requirements for student research projects.

title: Student Attitudes Toward Declaring Generative AI Use in Academic Writing in Nigerian Library Schools: A Cross-Sectional Survey
authors: Nkechi Anthonia Idoko; Opeyemi Rachael Oboh; Bolaji David Oladokun; Emenike Gabriel Chukwu; Juliana Akpan Benson
source_used: OpenAlex abstract; closed access (SAGE)
ft_reason: HE; reports actual (self-reported) GenAI declaration behaviour on assessed writing, which is evidence on declaration designs (b under Amendment 3); peer-reviewed.
sample: 374 LIS students across selected Nigerian universities

key_findings.finding: Students widely used AI tools for writing tasks but showed weak attitudes to declaring use, often declaring only when explicitly required; policy awareness was unrelated to attitudes.
Disclosure was shaped by fear of penalties, lecturer expectations, unclear guidelines and fear of negative judgement.

dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Unclear guidelines and fear of penalty limit disclosure.

author_recommendations: Integrate disclosure requirements into assessment practices, with clear policies and training (not tested)
limitations: Abstract only; self-report survey.
redesign_note: Evidence that voluntary declaration is low and inconsistent unless it is built into assessment.

title: ACADEMIC PERMISSIBILITY IN LLM-ASSISTED EFL WRITING: HOW CONTEXTUAL JUSTIFICATIONS SHAPE STUDENTS' MORAL JUDGMENTS IN A WITHIN-SUBJECTS VIGNETTE SURVEY
venue: International Journal of Education, Technology and Science
source_used: Zenodo record 22230040 (publisher deposit linked from DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22211397)
ft_reason: Under Amendment 3 this is c_not_redesign: a vignette survey of students' moral judgements about the acceptability of LLM use (integrity attitudes/perceptions only).
sample: 220 EFL students at three public universities in Laghouat, Algeria

key_findings.finding: Learning intent most raised perceived acceptability of LLM use (mean shift about 1.6, d about 0.7), while disclosure had only a small, non-robust effect; proofreading was rated most acceptable and paraphrasing least.

dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students' acceptability judgements hinge on learning intent and verification more than on disclosure.

author_recommendations: Writing tasks should require documenting how AI output was checked and revised (not tested)
limitations: Hypothetical vignette judgements, not observed behaviour.
redesign_note: Covers attitudes to LLM acceptability; only indirect implications for declaration design.
